chunks: From him, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Hammad, from Ibrahim ibn Abd Allah, from some of his freedmen, who said:

I asked him about the nocturnal emission of the fasting person. He said: If he emits semen during the day in the month of Ramadan, he is not permitted to sleep until he performs the ritual bath. And if he emits semen at night in the month of Ramadan, he should not sleep until he performs the ritual bath, except for a short while. Whoever becomes junub (in a state of major ritual impurity) in the month of Ramadan and sleeps until morning, then upon him is freeing a slave or feeding sixty poor people, and he must make up that day and complete his fasting, and it will never catch up to him (i.e., the missed day is not counted as part of the six days of Shawwal or similar compensations if applicable, but here implies the specific expiation is for the delay). The meaning in these narrations is that we interpret them as referring to one who deliberately leaves the bath until morning, for upon him is one of these expiations. And the first narrations include one who sleeps intending to bathe before dawn, but sleep continues until morning. There is no contradiction between them in any case, nor does that contradict [this interpretation].

key_terms.جُنُب: One in a state of major ritual impurity

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for a fasting person in Ramadan who sleeps until dawn without performing ghusl after a nocturnal emission?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves the apparent contradiction in the narrations by distinguishing between the general prohibition of sleeping before ghusl and the specific penalty for deliberately delaying it until dawn, which incurs the major expiation (kaffarah). This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the validity of the fast despite ritual impurity, provided the ghusl is performed before Fajr, while highlighting the spiritual weight of intentional negligence during Ramadan.
